body:
What makes a submarine different from a surface ship?

A submarine is a vessel designed to operate below the water's surface. It can change its buoyancy using ballast arrangements so that it can descend, remain submerged and surface when required. Its underwater operation makes acoustic detection, onboard power and air management especially important.

A surface ship can normally obtain air directly from the atmosphere for its engines. A submerged submarine cannot rely on atmospheric air in the same way. Its propulsion and power system strongly influence how long it can remain underwater.

Diesel-electric submarines

In a conventional diesel-electric submarine, diesel generators can provide electrical power and recharge batteries when sufficient atmospheric air is available. While submerged, the submarine may use stored electrical energy to power its propulsion and other systems.

Because diesel engines require oxygen for combustion, conventional diesel-electric submarines periodically need access to atmospheric air for battery recharging or other requirements. This may involve surfacing or using a snorkel, which permits air exchange while the submarine remains near the surface.

Battery-powered underwater operation can be relatively quiet, but battery energy is limited. A submarine's underwater endurance is therefore influenced by its power-storage and power-generation arrangements.

Nuclear-powered submarines

A nuclear-powered submarine uses heat from an onboard nuclear reactor to generate power. The reactor produces heat through nuclear fission and does not need atmospheric oxygen. Consequently, the submarine can remain submerged for long periods without surfacing merely to run an air-breathing propulsion engine. Its endurance is still affected by crew provisions, maintenance and other operational constraints.

Nuclear-powered describes propulsion; nuclear-armed describes the weapons carried. They are different characteristics. A nuclear-powered submarine is not automatically a ballistic-missile submarine, and a nuclear-powered attack submarine does not have to carry nuclear weapons.

Important submarine abbreviations

CategoryMeaningMain distinction
SSKConventional attack submarineGenerally diesel-electric propulsion
SSNNuclear-powered attack submarineNuclear propulsion; attack and sea-control roles
SSBNNuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarineNuclear propulsion; strategic deterrence role

The common abbreviations identify a submarine's general type. They should not be confused with an aircraft's UAV classification or a surface ship's frigate and destroyer categories.

Air-independent propulsion

Air-independent propulsion (AIP) is a propulsion or power-generation arrangement that allows a conventionally powered submarine to produce useful power while submerged without relying on a continuous supply of atmospheric air.

AIP can reduce the frequency with which a diesel-electric submarine must access atmospheric oxygen and thereby increase underwater endurance. Different AIP technologies exist. A fuel-cell-based arrangement produces electrical energy through an electrochemical process using carried reactants.

AIP is not the same as nuclear propulsion. An AIP-equipped conventional submarine remains dependent on its available fuel or stored reactants. It does not gain the practically extended reactor-powered operating endurance of a nuclear-powered submarine.

Indian submarines and the Gujarat connection

Project 75 comprises 6 Kalvari-class diesel-electric submarines. The 6th and final submarine, INS Vaghsheer, was commissioned on 15 January 2025. The class is a conventional submarine class, not an SSBN class.

INS Arighaat, the 2nd Arihant-class submarine, was commissioned on 29 August 2024 at Visakhapatnam. It belongs to India's nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine programme and supports the sea-based component of strategic deterrence.

On 24 October 2026, the Ministry of Defence announced the inauguration of Setting to Work Phase-2 activity for the indigenous AIP energy module developed by DRDO's Naval Materials Research Laboratory (NMRL). The activity took place at Larsen & Toubro's facility at Hazira, Gujarat.

According to the announcement, the next steps were to energise and test the module before its planned handover for integration into a Kalvari-class submarine in early 2027. Thus, at the 14 November 2026 content cutoff, the announcement established a development and testing milestone, not completion of the proposed submarine integration.

Prelims focus

  • SSK means a conventional attack submarine; SSN means a nuclear-powered attack submarine.
  • SSBN means a nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine.
  • INS Vaghsheer is the 6th Project 75 Kalvari-class diesel-electric submarine, commissioned on 15 January 2025.
  • INS Arighaat is the 2nd Arihant-class submarine, commissioned on 29 August 2024.
  • DRDO's NMRL developed the indigenous AIP module associated with the 24 October 2026 milestone at Hazira, Gujarat.
  • Trap: AIP is not nuclear propulsion, and the October 2026 milestone did not mean that integration planned for 2027 had already occurred.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Second Arihant-Class submarine INS Arighaat commissioned into Indian Navy', 29 August 2024; 'Indian Navy Set to Commission Three Frontline Fleet Assets Nilgiri, Surat and Vaghsheer', 1 January 2025; 'Indigenous AIP system for Indian Navy's diesel-electric submarines achieves key milestone with inauguration of Setting to Work Phase-2 Activity', 24 October 2026; consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Diesel-electric submarines use limited batteries underwater; AIP uses carried fuel or reactants; nuclear reactors support long endurance with operating limits.
pictures.caption: Conventional batteries, AIP and nuclear reactors provide different forms of underwater energy support.

title: Submarines: Types, Underwater Propulsion and India's AIP Programme

body:
Why sound is useful underwater

Underwater detection depends strongly on the physical properties of water. Ordinary radio waves used by many radars do not travel effectively through seawater over large distances. Sound, however, can propagate through water and carry information about objects that are not visible from the surface.

Sound is a mechanical wave produced by a disturbance in a material medium. It requires matter through which to travel and cannot propagate through a vacuum. When sound encounters an object, part of the sound energy may be reflected as an echo.

SONAR originally stands for Sound Navigation and Ranging. It uses underwater sound to detect or study objects and conditions in water.

Active and passive sonar

Active sonar

An active sonar transmits a sound pulse into water and listens for a reflected echo. The time between transmission and reception can help estimate how far away the reflecting object is, provided the sound's travel characteristics are taken into account.

Active sonar is useful when a direct acoustic measurement is required. Its important limitation is that the transmitted sound may also be detected by other listeners.

Passive sonar

A passive sonar listens to sounds already present in the water. Ships, submarines and other machinery can produce detectable acoustic signatures. Passive sonar does not need to transmit a sound pulse to receive information.

Passive listening can help detect and classify sound sources while avoiding an active transmission. However, a single passive observation does not normally provide a straightforward echo-based distance measurement. Additional observations or methods are needed to estimate distance reliably.

FeatureActive sonarPassive sonar
Sound transmissionTransmits a pulseDoes not transmit a search pulse
Information usedReflected echoSounds produced by sources
Distance measurementCan use echo travel timeRequires additional information or observations
Key limitationIts transmission may be detectedDepends on sounds that can be received

Where sonar equipment is installed

  • Hull-mounted sonar: Installed on the ship's hull to observe underwater conditions around the vessel.
  • Towed-array sonar: Uses acoustic sensors carried behind a vessel to receive underwater sound.
  • Dipping sonar: Can be lowered from a suitable helicopter into water for acoustic observation.
  • Sonobuoy: A buoy-based acoustic sensor, often placed from an aircraft, that provides information about underwater sounds or returns.

These names usually describe the sensor's installation or deployment method. They do not automatically indicate whether every system operates actively or passively.

Anti-submarine warfare as a coordinated task

Anti-submarine warfare (ASW) is the military field concerned with detecting, tracking and countering submarines. Its difficulty arises because submarines are below the surface and may be hard to observe directly.

ASW can involve surface warships, submarines, maritime patrol aircraft and helicopters. Their observations may be combined to improve awareness. Acoustic sensors detect underwater sound; radar and visual systems support broader observation of the sea and surface activity.

A torpedo is a self-propelled weapon designed to travel through water towards an underwater or surface target. A depth charge is a different type of underwater weapon. Both belong to naval warfare, but neither is a sonar sensor.

Indian sonar examples

DRDO has developed several indigenous naval acoustic systems, including the USHUS-2 sonar associated with submarines and the HUMSA family associated with surface ships. Its work has also included helicopter-borne dipping sonar technology.

India's maritime aviation includes the P-8I maritime patrol aircraft and shipborne anti-submarine helicopters. Their value comes from combining observation, communication and naval support rather than from any one sensor alone.

Prelims focus

  • SONAR means Sound Navigation and Ranging.
  • Sound requires a medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum.
  • Active sonar transmits sound and detects echoes; passive sonar listens for existing sounds.
  • Hull-mounted, towed-array and dipping sonar describe different equipment arrangements.
  • USHUS-2 is associated with submarines; HUMSA is associated with surface ships.
  • Trap: Sonar uses sound, whereas radar relies on electromagnetic waves.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Ch. 13, 'Sound'; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Ch. 12, 'Sound', sections on propagation and reflection; U.S. Navy, 'U.S. Navy Sonar', sections 'Passive Sonar' and 'Active Sonar'; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Republic Day Parade 2023: DRDO to showcase tableau on surveillance, communication & neutralizing threats', 24 January 2023; consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Active sonar sends a pulse and receives its reflected echo; passive sonar receives sound from a source without sending a search pulse.
pictures.caption: Active sonar sends a sound pulse and receives an echo; passive sonar listens without transmitting a pulse.

title: Sonar and Anti-Submarine Warfare: The Science of Detecting Objects Underwater

body:
Meaning of maritime-domain awareness

Maritime-domain awareness (MDA) is the understanding of activities, conditions and developments at sea that may affect maritime safety, security, economic activity or national interests.

Seas contain merchant vessels, fishing boats, naval ships and many other activities. Authorities need to understand which vessels are present, where they are moving and whether an observed activity needs attention. This requires several kinds of information because no single sensor can observe every vessel or reliably explain every movement.

Important sources of maritime information

Coastal and shipborne radar

Radar uses electromagnetic waves to detect objects and estimate their position and movement. Coastal radars help monitor vessels in the surrounding maritime area. Radar detection does not automatically establish the name, ownership or purpose of a vessel.

Automatic Identification System

The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is used by appropriately equipped ships to exchange information such as vessel identity, position, course and speed with other ships and shore stations.

Under international maritime safety rules, AIS carriage is required on ships of 300 gross tonnage and above on international voyages, cargo ships of 500 gross tonnage and above on other voyages, and all passenger ships irrespective of size, subject to permitted exemptions. It is not carried by every small boat. An AIS message is information transmitted by the vessel's equipment; it should not be treated as independent proof of every claim made by that equipment.

Satellite and aerial observation

Satellites can provide observations over large maritime areas. Aircraft and UAVs can also contribute imagery and other sensor information. Surface patrols, port authorities and reports from coastal communities can provide additional context.

Why information must be combined

Suppose a coastal radar detects a moving vessel. AIS may help identify it if the vessel has an operating transponder and its data are available. A patrol or other observation may provide further confirmation. If the vessel has no available AIS information, that alone does not prove unlawful activity: its size, type, equipment and circumstances must be considered.

Combining observations from different sources is called information fusion. Its purpose is to create a more reliable picture than any isolated report can provide. Fusion also helps identify contradictory information and avoid counting the same observation several times.

India's Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region

The Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR) was inaugurated on 22 December 2018 at the Information Management and Analysis Centre (IMAC), Gurugram. It supports the exchange and analysis of maritime information with relevant partners to improve awareness of activities in the Indian Ocean Region.

The centre is concerned with information and maritime security cooperation. It is not an aircraft carrier, a radar station on a single ship or a submarine command system.

Why maritime surveillance matters to Gujarat

Gujarat has a long coastline on the Arabian Sea, including the Gulf of Kutch and Gulf of Khambhat. Maritime activity includes commercial shipping, ports and fishing. Coastal surveillance is therefore relevant to the state's economic activity and maritime safety.

For Gujarat, the principle is the same as elsewhere: information from coastal observation, vessel identification, shipping authorities and other sources must be interpreted together. A radar contact, an AIS report and a verified vessel identity are related but different pieces of information.

Prelims focus

  • Radar detects objects using electromagnetic waves; sonar uses underwater sound.
  • AIS stands for Automatic Identification System.
  • AIS can transmit a ship's identity, position, course and speed.
  • IFC-IOR was inaugurated on 22 December 2018 at IMAC, Gurugram.
  • Gujarat's Arabian Sea coast makes maritime monitoring relevant to ports and fishing activity.
  • Trap: The absence of AIS information does not, by itself, establish that a vessel is engaged in unlawful activity.

[Sources: International Maritime Organization, 'AIS Transponders', sections 'Regulations for carriage of AIS' and 'Maritime security – AIS ship data'; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Raksha Mantri Inaugurates Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR)', 22 December 2018; consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Radar, AIS and other observations feed information fusion to form a more reliable maritime picture; radar alone cannot identify a vessel.
pictures.caption: Maritime-domain awareness combines several information sources into a more reliable picture of activity at sea.

title: Maritime-Domain Awareness: Radar, AIS and Information Fusion
